# @argszero/cordis-plugin-tool-deadline-guard

A cordis plugin for the DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`)
that puts a deadline on tool calls that declare non

e — the calls for which
nothing in the harness arms anything today.
[代码示例省略，未执行]

A tool call is bounded exactly when its own definition says so.
`ToolDefinition.timeoutMs` is option

al ("Cooperative tool-call timeout budget in
milliseconds. Omit for no deadline"), and the core enfo

rcer
(`@deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-call-timeout-policy`, mounted by the base bundle) opens
with `if (timeo

utMs === undefined) return next()`. Omit the field and *nothing
arms anything* — not a timer, not a
signal, not a diagnostic.

That omission is the norm rather than the exception. Of the 40 non-test source
files calling `define

Tool(` at `dsh-v0.1.6-alpha.2`, **26 contain no `timeoutMs`
at all** — 25 shipped tool modules plus

the test fixture helper — among them
`tool-subagent` (delegation), `mcp-resources` (tools owned by s

omeone else's
server), `tool-terminal`, `tool-ask-user`, the fs read/write/edit tools, and
`tool-wor

kflow` / `tool-ralph` / `tool-todo` / `plan-mode`. Two of those are
exactly where a long-horizon run

spends its time: a delegation whose child never
settles, and a tool on the far side of a network bo

its time: a delegation whose child never
settles, and a tool on the far side of a network boundary.

The symptom is not an error. It is a turn that keeps rendering as running with
nothing anywhere to e

xplain it. Compare the model call: the provider adapters
announce a stall (`DEFAULT_STREAM_IDLE_TIME

OUT_MS` = 300_000, re-armed per chunk
by `idleWatchdog`), so **silence is the signature of a wedged

tool call, not a
wedged model call**. Reported as discussion

#7339
("long-horizon tasks stall with nothing in the output"), and adjacent to

#6226 (a
foreground `subagent` call whose child process had already exited).
Mounted, the same call ends with something the model can act on:
[代码示例省略，未执行]

**0.2.0 adds the other half.** A call can also hang *before* it is dispatched,
where no declared bud

get and no `tools/execute` wrapper can reach it — see
The other half. The
same mount now covers that

phase too, under its own code
(`TOOL_PRE_EXECUTE_DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`), so a deployment can tell a bo

dy that ran
too long from a body that never ran at all.

## What it does, precisely

The plugin mounts on two documented public seams — `tools/execute` (the same one
the core policy use

s) and `tools/pre-execute` (the phase in front of it) — and
for each dispatch:

1. **Resolves the tool's own definition** (`ctx.tools.get(exec.name, exec.agent)`)
and decides wheth

er to arm at all. An unknown tool is the registry's business
(`UNKNOWN_TOOL`), and there is no defin

ition to weigh a budget against.
2. **Arms one timer and one controller**, and hands the tool a fuse

d signal
(`AbortSignal.any([caller, own])`) through `exec.signal`, exactly as the core
policy hands

it its derived deadline.
3. **Restores the caller's signal in a `finally`**, so post-execute listene

rs and
every later wrapper never see this mount's (possibly already-aborted) signal —
the rule the c

ore policy documents for the same reason.
4. **Substitutes a result only when its own timer fired.**

A call that settles
inside its budget returns the tool's own result object, unchanged: no
re-dispat

ch, no wrapper, no diagnostic.
5. **Races the pre-dispatch phase on the same kind of timer** and den

ies the call
if that phase is the thing that hung; a phase that settles inside its budget
dispatches

the call untouched, and a phase that fails on its own keeps the
registry's own error path.

An expired body budget produces the shape the loop already understands —
`isError: true` with `error

.info.code === 'TOOL_DEADLINE_EXCEEDED'` — under a
code **this plugin owns**, deliberately not the c

ore policy's `TOOL_TIMEOUT`: a
deployment can then tell "the tool declared a budget and blew it" fro

m "this
mount supplied a budget the tool never declared", which is the difference
between a tool bug

and a deployment policy. `ToolTimeoutError`-style routing on
`TOOL_TIMEOUT` keeps working for decla

red tools and does not silently capture
these.

An expired **pre-dispatch** phase is a different fact, so it gets a different
code (`TOOL_PRE_EXECUT

E_DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`) and a different shape (`deny`, not a
replaced result). See the next section.
## Compatibility

Requires `tools/execute`, `tools/pre-execute`, `ToolDispatchExecution`,
`PreToolDecision`, `ToolDefi

nition.timeoutMs` and `ctx.tools.get(name, agent)`,
all present in `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools` from `0.

1.2-rc.1` onward. The suite is run
against two lines besides its own build — `0.1.7-rc.2` (+ `cordis

` 4.0.4) and
`0.2.1-alpha.2` (+ `cordis` 4.0.5-alpha.1); 26/26 each. `@deepseek-ai/cordis` is a
peer
; `@deepseek-ai/schemastery` is the only runtime dependency.

The peer ranges are written as one explicit segment per release line, because a
prerelease range is

read two ways: npm excludes a prerelease unless a comparator
in the range names the same version tup

le, while pnpm passes `includePrerelease`
and admits more for the same string. A range that only nam

es the line it was
written on therefore installs under one package manager and `ERESOLVE`s under the

other — with the divergence made of exactly the releases people run on.
`probe-peer-range.mjs` is t

he audit, and `test/packaging.spec.mjs` pins its
result.
